ety.text: PIE word *h₁en Preposition and verb from Middle English in, from Old English in, from Proto-Germanic *in. Adverb, noun and adjective from Middle English in, from Old English inn and inne, from Proto-Germanic *innai. Sense 1/2 "in"/"into" are from the original PIE prefix, with locative/accusative case respectively. Sense 3/4 "qualification"/"means" are from the PIE metaphor of all infinitives coming from locatives.

senses.d: Contained by; inside.
ex: The dog is in the kennel.
There were three pickles in a jar.

senses.d: Within the bounds or limits of.
ex: I like living in the city.
There are lots of trees in the park.

senses.d: Surrounded by; among; amidst.
ex: We are in the enemy camp.
Her plane is in the air.

senses.d: Wearing (an item of clothing).
ex: I glanced over at the pretty girl in the red dress.
Who’s the blonde in the sunhat over there?

senses.d: Expressing abstract containment.
ex: There wasn't much of interest in her speech.
He hasn't got an original idea in him.

senses.d: Part of; a member of; out of; from among.
ex: You are one in a million.
She's in an orchestra.

senses.d: During (a period of time or event).
ex: My birthday is in the first week of December.
Easter falls in the fourth lunar month.

senses.d: Within (a certain elapsed time); by the end of.
ex: Will you be able to finish this in a week?
The massacre resulted in over 1000 deaths in three hours.

senses.d: At the end of (a period of time).
ex: They said they would call us in a week.

senses.d: Participating in a field, activity or industry.
ex: I've always worked in plastics.
She dabbles in Buddhism.

senses.d: To enclose.
To take in; to harvest.
ex: He that ears my land spares my team and gives me leave to in the crop.

senses.d: At or towards the interior of a defined space, such as a building or room.
ex: Suddenly a strange man walked in.
Would you like that to take away or eat in?

senses.d: Towards the speaker or other reference point.
ex: They flew in from London last night.
For six hours the tide flows in, then for another six hours it flows out.

senses.d: So as to be enclosed or surrounded by something.
ex: Bring the water to the boil and drop the vegetables in.
I was tired enough to snuggle in with the dogs on the couch and sleep there.

senses.d: After the beginning of something.
ex: The show still didn't become interesting 20 minutes in.

senses.d: Denotes a gathering of people assembled for the stated activity, sometimes, though not always, suggesting a protest.
ex: sing-in, pray-in, hug-in; see also be-in, love-in, sit-in, teach-in.

senses.d: A position of power or influence, or a way to get it.
ex: His parents got him an in with the company.

senses.d: One who, or that which, is in; especially, one who is in office.
The state of a batter/batsman who is currently batting; see innings.
Located indoors, especially at home or at one's office or place of work.
ex: Is Mr. Smith in?

senses.d: Located inside something.
ex: Little by little I pushed the snake into the basket, until finally all of it was in.
The bullet is about five centimetres in.

senses.d: Falling or remaining within the bounds of the playing area.
ex: If the tennis ball bounces on the line then it's in.

senses.d: Inserted or fitted into something.
ex: I've discovered why the TV wasn't working – the plug wasn't in!

senses.d: Having been collected or received.
ex: The replies to the questionnaires are now all in.

senses.d: In stock, available in stores (particularly of a new item).
ex: Our latest product is in!

senses.d: In fashion; popular.
ex: Skirts are in this year.

Pierce a new hole
If Hell was in you'd give your soul
To the great southern trendkill

senses.d: Incoming.
ex: the in train

senses.d: Furled or stowed.
Of the tide, at or near its highest level.
ex: You can't get round the headland when the tide's in.

fr:dans.gl: in, inside (enclosed in a physical space, a group, a state)

ety.text: Inherited from Old French denz, from Vulgar Latin dē intus, from Latin dē + intus, meaning "from inside" or "from within".
Inherited from Old Spanish en, from Latin in, from Old Latin en, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én.
From Old Galician-Portuguese en, from Latin in (“in”), from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”). Doublet of in.

pt:dentro de.gl: within; inside; in (in a place or spatial enclosure)

ety.text: According to Coromines and Pascual, from Old Spanish fazia (attested ca. 1300), with the variant faza (att. in Cid, Berceo, Calila e Dimna), and in pre-literary Latinized spelling faze ad (att. 1208, in a legal document), from Latin faciem ad (facing towards).

fr:en.gl: in (used to indicate space, also see usage notes)

ety.text: From Middle French en, from Old French en, from Latin in, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”).
From Latin intrā, with influence from Latin inter.
